Reference: Lee and Card (2008)

Model Setting

The paper studies inference in regression discontinuity (RD) designs in which the covariate that determines treatment is discrete or reported in coarse intervals, such as age in months or years, quarter of birth or enrollment counts. With a continuous covariate, no functional form is needed: one compares mean outcomes in neighbourhoods of the threshold whose width shrinks with the sample size, which is the basis of the nonparametric and semiparametric estimators of Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (2001) and Porter (2003). With discrete support there is an irreducible gap between the last control cell and the first treated cell, so even an infinite sample contains no observations arbitrarily close to the threshold. The researcher must choose a parametric form for the regression function, and the treatment effect is identified only by extrapolating that form to the threshold. The treatment effect is not nonparametrically identified.

The proposal is to treat the deviation of the true conditional expectation from the chosen parametric function at each support point as a random specification error. Three consequences follow. First, the specification error is a common component for all observations in a cell, so the regression error has a random-effects (group) structure of the kind analysed by Moulton (1990), conventional heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors overstate precision, and standard errors must at least be clustered on the distinct values of the covariate. Second, because an RD estimate is the difference of two extrapolations to the threshold, a further forecast-error term appears when the specification errors of the two counterfactual functions are not identical; the variance must then be increased by twice the variance of the specification error. Third, in that case the cell mean at the threshold carries information that least squares does not use optimally, and a shrinkage estimator that combines it with the regression prediction is more efficient; its confidence interval is a Bayesian (Empirical Bayes) posterior interval. The degree to which standard errors are inflated is tied to a goodness-of-fit statistic for the parametric form. The published article is purely methodological: it has no empirical application, no data set and no tables of estimates, and refers to applied work only for motivation.

D=1[X≥x0],Y=DY1+(1−D)Y0(1)D=1[X\geq x_0],\qquad Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0 \tag{1}D=1[X≥x0​],Y=DY1​+(1−D)Y0​(1)

When the support of XXX is continuous and E[Y1∣X=x]E[Y_1|X=x]E[Y1​∣X=x] and E[Y0∣X=x]E[Y_0|X=x]E[Y0​∣X=x] are continuous in xxx at x0x_0x0​, the effect is identified by the discontinuity of the regression function of the observed outcome:

E[Y∣X=x0]−lim⁡e→0+E[Y∣X=x0−e]=E[Y1∣X=x0]−lim⁡e→0+E[Y0∣X=x0−e]=E[Y1−Y0∣X=x0](2)\begin{aligned} E[Y|X=x_0]-\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y|X=x_0-e]&=E[Y_1|X=x_0]-\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y_0|X=x_0-e]\\ &=E[Y_1-Y_0|X=x_0] \end{aligned} \tag{2}E[Y∣X=x0​]−e→0+lim​E[Y∣X=x0​−e]​=E[Y1​∣X=x0​]−e→0+lim​E[Y0​∣X=x0​−e]=E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=x0​]​(2)

The data never reveal the counterfactual mean E[Y0∣X=x0]E[Y_0|X=x_0]E[Y0​∣X=x0​], but E[Y0∣X=x0−e]E[Y_0|X=x_0-e]E[Y0​∣X=x0​−e] approximates it arbitrarily well for small eee. Parametric Estimation and the Goodness-of-Fit Statistic

Common practice is to regress YYY on a low-order polynomial in xjx_jxj​ and the indicator DjD_jDj​. If the polynomial is the correct form of h(⋅)h(\cdot)h(⋅), conventional least squares inference is appropriate. Discreteness makes the functional form testable, because the polynomial model is nested in the saturated model with one dummy per support point. The goodness-of-fit statistic is:

G≡(ESSR−ESSUR)/(J−K)ESSUR/(N−J)(5)G\equiv\frac{(ESS_R-ESS_{UR})/(J-K)}{ESS_{UR}/(N-J)} \tag{5}G≡ESSUR​/(N−J)(ESSR​−ESSUR​)/(J−K)​(5)

where ESSRESS_RESSR​ is the restricted error sum of squares from the polynomial regression, ESSURESS_{UR}ESSUR​ is the unrestricted sum of squares from regressing YijY_{ij}Yij​ on a full set of dummies for the JJJ values of XXX, KKK is the number of parameters of the restricted model and NNN is the number of observations. Under normal and homoskedastic εij\varepsilon_{ij}εij​, GGG is distributed as F(J−K,N−J)F(J-K,N-J)F(J−K,N−J); without normality (J−K)⋅G(J-K)\cdot G(J−K)⋅G is asymptotically χ2(J−K)\chi^2(J-K)χ2(J−K). Under heteroskedasticity across cells the statistic is replaced by a weighted version:

G~=∑j=1Jnjσ^εj2(Y‾j−Wjθ^)2,σ^εj2=1nj∑i=1nj(Yij−Y‾j)2(6)\tilde{G}=\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{n_j}{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}}\left(\overline{Y}_j-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2,\qquad\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}=\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\left(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j\right)^2 \tag{6}G~=j=1∑J​σ^εj2​nj​​(Yj​−Wj​θ^)2,σ^εj2​=nj​1​i=1∑nj​​(Yij​−Yj​)2(6)

where njn_jnj​ is the number of observations in cell jjj, Y‾j\overline{Y}_jYj​ is the cell mean, WjW_jWj​ is the row vector of regressors and θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ the least squares coefficient vector; G~\tilde{G}G~ is asymptotically χ2(J−K)\chi^2(J-K)χ2(J−K) (exactly so when the cells are weighted by the inverse of their estimated error variances). This is a minimum-distance form: it measures the weighted distance between the unrestricted cell means and the fitted values of the parametric model.

A rejection does not imply that the least squares estimate β^\hat{\beta}β^​ is inconsistent for β0\beta_0β0​. Following White (1980) and Chamberlain (1994), β^\hat{\beta}β^​ is consistent for β∗\beta^*β∗, the discontinuity in the least squares approximation to the true regression function, and conventional heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors are appropriate for inference about β∗\beta^*β∗. The difference between β∗\beta^*β∗ and β0\beta_0β0​ is unknown and may be small or zero. It is nevertheless natural to be more sceptical of β^\hat{\beta}β^​ as an estimate of β0\beta_0β0​ when GGG rejects and more confident when GGG is close to 1. The procedures below formalize this by inflating standard errors by an amount directly related to GGG.

Random Specification Error

Suppose a polynomial is chosen to approximate h(⋅)h(\cdot)h(⋅). The micro-data regression becomes:

Yij=α0+Djβ0+Xjγ0+aj+εij(7)Y_{ij}=\alpha_0+D_j\beta_0+X_j\gamma_0+a_j+\varepsilon_{ij} \tag{7}Yij​=α0​+Dj​β0​+Xj​γ0​+aj​+εij​(7)

where XjX_jXj​ is a row vector of polynomial terms in xjx_jxj​ (which may include interactions with DjD_jDj​, so that the derivatives of the regression function can differ on the two sides) and aj≡h(xj)−Xjγ0a_j\equiv h(x_j)-X_j\gamma_0aj​≡h(xj​)−Xj​γ0​ is the specification error, the deviation of the true function from the polynomial at support point jjj. The paper treats the sharp design without individual-level covariates; in a valid RD design such covariates can be omitted just as baseline covariates can be omitted in a randomized experiment.

The first procedure treats aja_jaj​ as random and orthogonal to XXX, that is, E[aj∣X=xj]=0E[a_j|X=x_j]=0E[aj​∣X=xj​]=0 for j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J. Two implications follow. Least squares remains consistent for β0\beta_0β0​, since the composite error aj+εija_j+\varepsilon_{ij}aj​+εij​ is mean independent of the regressors. And aja_jaj​ is a random effect shared by all observations in cell jjj, which induces within-cell correlation of the error. Heteroskedasticity-consistent variance estimators assume independent errors across observations and are therefore inconsistent for the variance of β^\hat{\beta}β^​; as in Moulton (1990), where a regressor varies only at the group level, they understate it. The orthogonality assumption is strong, but conventional parametric inference imposes the strictly stronger assumption aj=0a_j=0aj​=0.

Identical Specification Errors

Clustered standard errors may still understate the variability of β^\hat{\beta}β^​, because estimating the discontinuity amounts to using data away from the threshold to forecast two means at the threshold. Approximate the two counterfactual functions by:

E[Y1∣X=xj]=α0+Xjγ0+β0+a1jE[Y0∣X=xj]=α0+Xjγ0+a0j(13)\begin{aligned} E[Y_1|X=x_j]&=\alpha_0+X_j\gamma_0+\beta_0+a_{1j}\\ E[Y_0|X=x_j]&=\alpha_0+X_j\gamma_0+a_{0j} \end{aligned} \tag{13}E[Y1​∣X=xj​]E[Y0​∣X=xj​]​=α0​+Xj​γ0​+β0​+a1j​=α0​+Xj​γ0​+a0j​​(13)

where a1ja_{1j}a1j​ and a0ja_{0j}a0j​ are the random specification errors of the two approximations. If a1j=a0ja_{1j}=a_{0j}a1j​=a0j​, then Y=DY1+(1−D)Y0Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0Y=DY1​+(1−D)Y0​ gives:

E[Y∣X=xj]=α0+Xjγ0+Djβ0+aj,aj≡Dja1j+(1−Dj)a0j(14)E[Y|X=x_j]=\alpha_0+X_j\gamma_0+D_j\beta_0+a_j,\qquad a_j\equiv D_ja_{1j}+(1-D_j)a_{0j} \tag{14}E[Y∣X=xj​]=α0​+Xj​γ0​+Dj​β0​+aj​,aj​≡Dj​a1j​+(1−Dj​)a0j​(14)

which is the random-effects regression above. Then β0=E[Y1−Y0∣X=xk]\beta_0=E[Y_1-Y_0|X=x_k]β0​=E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=xk​], the treatment effect at the threshold is deterministic, and the clustered variance is appropriate. The assumption of identical specification errors says that the same approximation error would arise whether or not the threshold cell were assigned to treatment. It is plausible when the source of the error is unrelated to treatment. The paper's example is Card and Shore-Sheppard (2004), who relate Medicaid enrollment to quarter of birth: seasonal health differences by quarter of birth would be present with or without the eligibility expansion. The errors can be identical even when the counterfactual functions are not parallel. With side-specific polynomial coefficients γ1∗\gamma^*_1γ1∗​ and γ0∗\gamma^*_0γ0∗​:

E[Y∣X=xj]=α0+Xjγ0∗+XjDj(γ1∗−γ0∗)+Djβ0+ajE[Y1−Y0∣X=xj]=Xj(γ1∗−γ0∗)+β0(15)\begin{aligned} E[Y|X=x_j]&=\alpha_0+X_j\gamma^*_0+X_jD_j\left(\gamma^*_1-\gamma^*_0\right)+D_j\beta_0+a_j\\ E[Y_1-Y_0|X=x_j]&=X_j\left(\gamma^*_1-\gamma^*_0\right)+\beta_0 \end{aligned} \tag{15}E[Y∣X=xj​]E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=xj​]​=α0​+Xj​γ0∗​+Xj​Dj​(γ1∗​−γ0∗​)+Dj​β0​+aj​=Xj​(γ1∗​−γ0∗​)+β0​​(15)

so the regression includes interactions of DjD_jDj​ with the polynomial terms, and the treatment effect function is itself a polynomial in XXX. This fully interacted specification requires that, even if each counterfactual function is only approximated by a polynomial, the difference between them is described by a polynomial without error (at least at X=xkX=x_kX=xk​).

Relation to Bayesian Estimation

The combination estimator can be rewritten as β∗=[λY‾k+(1−λ)(α^+β^)]−α^\beta^*=[\lambda\overline{Y}_k+(1-\lambda)(\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta})]-\hat{\alpha}β∗=[λYk​+(1−λ)(α^+β^​)]−α^: the bracket is a λ\lambdaλ-weighted average of the cell mean and the regression prediction, an estimate of E[Y1∣X=0]E[Y_1|X=0]E[Y1​∣X=0], and α^\hat{\alpha}α^ estimates E[Y0∣X=0]E[Y_0|X=0]E[Y0​∣X=0]. Consider the likelihood Yik∼N(E[Y1∣X=0],σ2)Y_{ik}\sim N(E[Y_1|X=0],\sigma^2)Yik​∼N(E[Y1​∣X=0],σ2) with σ2\sigma^2σ2 known, and independent normal priors for E[Y1∣X=xk]E[Y_1|X=x_k]E[Y1​∣X=xk​] and E[Y0∣X=xk]E[Y_0|X=x_k]E[Y0​∣X=xk​] with means E1E_1E1​, E0E_0E0​ and variances σ12\sigma^2_1σ12​, σ02\sigma^2_0σ02​. The posterior of E[Y1∣X=xk]E[Y_1|X=x_k]E[Y1​∣X=xk​] is N(λY‾k+(1−λ)E1,(1−λ)σ12)N(\lambda\overline{Y}_k+(1-\lambda)E_1,(1-\lambda)\sigma^2_1)N(λYk​+(1−λ)E1​,(1−λ)σ12​) with λ=σ12/(σ2/nk+σ12)\lambda=\sigma^2_1/(\sigma^2/n_k+\sigma^2_1)λ=σ12​/(σ2/nk​+σ12​), the posterior of E[Y0∣X=xk]E[Y_0|X=x_k]E[Y0​∣X=xk​] equals its prior because there are no untreated data at X=0X=0X=0, and the posterior of the treatment effect is:

E[Y1−Y0∣X=0] ∼ N([λY‾k+(1−λ)E1]−E0, σ12+σ02−λ2(σ2nk+σ12))(29)E[Y_1-Y_0|X=0]\ \sim\ N\left(\left[\lambda\overline{Y}_k+(1-\lambda)E_1\right]-E_0,\ \sigma^2_1+\sigma^2_0-\lambda^2\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{n_k}+\sigma^2_1\right)\right) \tag{29}E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=0] ∼ N([λYk​+(1−λ)E1​]−E0​, σ12​+σ02​−λ2(nk​σ2​+σ12​))(29)

With a diffuse prior on E[Y0∣X=0]E[Y_0|X=0]E[Y0​∣X=0] the posterior is uninformative: without outside information the threshold cell alone says nothing about the treatment effect. The data away from the threshold supply the prior. Setting E1=α^+β^E_1=\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}E1​=α^+β^​ and σ12=V(α^+β^)^+σ^a2\sigma^2_1=\widehat{V(\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta})}+\hat{\sigma}^2_aσ12​=V(α^+β^​)​+σ^a2​ from a regression on the data to the right of the kkkth cell, E0=α^E_0=\hat{\alpha}E0​=α^ and σ02=V(α^)^+σ^a2\sigma^2_0=\widehat{V(\hat{\alpha})}+\hat{\sigma}^2_aσ02​=V(α^)​+σ^a2​ from a regression on the data to the left, and replacing σ2\sigma^2σ2 by σ^ε2\hat{\sigma}^2_\varepsilonσ^ε2​, the posterior is N(β^∗,V(β^∗)^)N(\hat{\beta}^*,\widehat{V(\hat{\beta}^*)})N(β^​∗,V(β^​∗)​) for the fully interacted model. The bracketed estimate of E[Y1∣X=xk]E[Y_1|X=x_k]E[Y1​∣X=xk​] is a shrinkage (Stein) estimator, and the confidence intervals are Empirical Bayes intervals. A hierarchical alternative would place a prior on the hyperparameters α0\alpha_0α0​, β0\beta_0β0​, γ0\gamma_0γ0​, σa2\sigma^2_aσa2​ and the sampling variances.

Fuzzy Designs

With imperfect compliance the expected treatment, not the treatment itself, jumps at the threshold; the paper's example is the class-size rule of Angrist and Lavy. The extension adds specification errors to a two-equation system:

Y1ij=Djδ0+Xjγ1+a1j+uijY2ij=Y1ijβ0+Xjγ2+a2j+vij(30)\begin{aligned} Y_{1ij}&=D_j\delta_0+X_j\gamma_1+a_{1j}+u_{ij}\\ Y_{2ij}&=Y_{1ij}\beta_0+X_j\gamma_2+a_{2j}+v_{ij} \end{aligned} \tag{30}Y1ij​Y2ij​​=Dj​δ0​+Xj​γ1​+a1j​+uij​=Y1ij​β0​+Xj​γ2​+a2j​+vij​​(30)

where (Y1ij,Y2ij)(Y_{1ij},Y_{2ij})(Y1ij​,Y2ij​) are the observed treatment and outcome of individual iii in cell jjj, δ0\delta_0δ0​ is the discontinuity in Y1Y_1Y1​ at X=0X=0X=0, β0\beta_0β0​ is the causal effect of Y1Y_1Y1​ on Y2Y_2Y2​, (uij,vij)(u_{ij},v_{ij})(uij​,vij​) are potentially correlated errors and (a1j,a2j)(a_{1j},a_{2j})(a1j​,a2j​) is an i.i.d. vector of mean-zero random specification errors (in this block the subscripts 1 and 2 index equations, not potential outcomes). Instrumenting Y1ijY_{1ij}Y1ij​ with DjD_jDj​, which is assumed to have no direct effect on Y2Y_2Y2​, equals the ratio of the two estimated discontinuities and remains asymptotically unbiased for β0\beta_0β0​, but conventional instrumental variables standard errors ignore the group structure of the residuals and overstate precision (Shore-Sheppard 1996); clustering on the values of XXX is again the remedy. This system embodies identical specification errors. With independent errors, the procedure for the sharp design is applied to each outcome, giving estimates β^\hat{\beta}β^​ and π^\hat{\pi}π^ of E[Y11−Y10∣X=0]E[Y^1_1-Y^0_1|X=0]E[Y11​−Y10​∣X=0] and E[Y21−Y20∣X=0]E[Y^1_2-Y^0_2|X=0]E[Y21​−Y20​∣X=0] (superscripts denote potential outcomes), and:

(β^−E[Y11−Y10∣X=0], π^−E[Y21−Y20∣X=0])′Σ^−1(β^−E[Y11−Y10∣X=0], π^−E[Y21−Y20∣X=0])→dχ2(2)(31)\left(\hat{\beta}-E[Y^1_1-Y^0_1|X=0],\ \hat{\pi}-E[Y^1_2-Y^0_2|X=0]\right)'\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}\left(\hat{\beta}-E[Y^1_1-Y^0_1|X=0],\ \hat{\pi}-E[Y^1_2-Y^0_2|X=0]\right)\xrightarrow{d}\chi^2(2) \tag{31}(β^​−E[Y11​−Y10​∣X=0], π^−E[Y21​−Y20​∣X=0])′Σ^−1(β^​−E[Y11​−Y10​∣X=0], π^−E[Y21​−Y20​∣X=0])d​χ2(2)(31)

where Σ^\hat{\Sigma}Σ^ is a consistent estimator of the variance matrix of the error vector, including the covariances of the estimation errors and of the specification errors across the two outcomes. Inverting the statistic gives a joint 95% confidence set for the two discontinuities and, from it, a confidence set for their ratio.

Recommended Procedure and Scope

The paper summarizes its proposal in four steps.

  • Step 1: normalize XXX so that the threshold is at 0 (the intercept then estimates E[Y0∣X=0]E[Y_0|X=0]E[Y0​∣X=0]), choose the parametric form, and run the regression on the micro data with both heteroskedasticity-consistent and cluster-consistent standard errors, clustering on the values of XXX.

  • Step 2: decide whether the specification errors in E[Y1∣X=xk]E[Y_1|X=x_k]E[Y1​∣X=xk​] and E[Y0∣X=xk]E[Y_0|X=x_k]E[Y0​∣X=xk​] can be taken as identical. If so, use the clustered standard errors.

  • Step 3: if not, collapse the data to cell means, variances and counts, run the cell-size-weighted regression (the point estimate and the heteroskedasticity-consistent standard error should reproduce step 1 up to a finite-sample correction), compute σ^a2\hat{\sigma}^2_aσ^a2​ from the regression mean squared error and the cell variances, and add 2σ^a22\hat{\sigma}^2_a2σ^a2​ to the sampling variance.

  • Step 4: for more efficiency, use the estimated variances and covariances of the discontinuity coefficient and the intercept and the variance of the kkkth cell to compute λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^, β^∗\hat{\beta}^*β^​∗ and V(β^∗)^\widehat{V(\hat{\beta}^*)}V(β^​∗)​.

The procedure does not settle how to choose the systematic part of the functional form, such as the order of the polynomial; it only acknowledges that whatever form is chosen may be wrong. There is no empirical illustration in the article: no data are analysed and no estimates or standard errors, clustered or otherwise, are reported. The only empirical content is the motivation (programs such as Medicare and Medicaid with age-based eligibility where age is recorded in months or years) and the two examples cited above.

References

  • Lee, David S and David Card. 2008. “Regression Discontinuity Inference with Specification Error.” Journal of Econometrics, 142(2): 655–674.

This equation defines the sharp regression discontinuity design. XXX is the observed covariate that determines treatment (age, date of birth, enrollment), x0x_0x0​ is the known threshold, and DDD is the treatment indicator, a deterministic step function of XXX: everybody with X≥x0X\geq x_0X≥x0​ is treated and nobody with X<x0X<x_0X<x0​ is. Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​ are the potential outcomes with and without treatment; only one of them is observed for each individual, and the second part of the equation is the switching rule that says which one.

Two things follow directly. First, because DDD is a function of XXX, there is no variation in treatment conditional on XXX, so the effect cannot be estimated by comparing treated and untreated units with the same XXX; one must compare units on the two sides of x0x_0x0​. Second, taking conditional expectations of the switching rule gives the observed regression function on each side:

E[Y∣X=x]={E[Y1∣X=x],x≥x0E[Y0∣X=x],x<x0E[Y|X=x]=\begin{cases}E[Y_1|X=x], & x\geq x_0\\ E[Y_0|X=x], & x<x_0\end{cases}E[Y∣X=x]={E[Y1​∣X=x],E[Y0​∣X=x],​x≥x0​x<x0​​

The data therefore reveal E[Y1∣X=x]E[Y_1|X=x]E[Y1​∣X=x] only to the right of the threshold and E[Y0∣X=x]E[Y_0|X=x]E[Y0​∣X=x] only to the left. This is the input of equation (2), and the reason why the counterfactual mean E[Y0∣X=x0]E[Y_0|X=x_0]E[Y0​∣X=x0​] must be obtained by a limit (continuous XXX) or by extrapolation of a parametric form (discrete XXX, equations (3) and (7)).

Start from equation (1). At X=x0X=x_0X=x0​ the indicator is D=1D=1D=1, so Y=Y1Y=Y_1Y=Y1​ and

E[Y∣X=x0]=E[Y1∣X=x0]E[Y|X=x_0]=E[Y_1|X=x_0]E[Y∣X=x0​]=E[Y1​∣X=x0​]

For any e>0e>0e>0 the point x0−ex_0-ex0​−e lies below the threshold, so D=0D=0D=0, Y=Y0Y=Y_0Y=Y0​ and E[Y∣X=x0−e]=E[Y0∣X=x0−e]E[Y|X=x_0-e]=E[Y_0|X=x_0-e]E[Y∣X=x0​−e]=E[Y0​∣X=x0​−e]. Taking the limit from the left,

lim⁡e→0+E[Y∣X=x0−e]=lim⁡e→0+E[Y0∣X=x0−e]\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y|X=x_0-e]=\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y_0|X=x_0-e]e→0+lim​E[Y∣X=x0​−e]=e→0+lim​E[Y0​∣X=x0​−e]

Subtracting gives the first line of the equation. For the second line use the continuity of E[Y0∣X=x]E[Y_0|X=x]E[Y0​∣X=x] in xxx at x0x_0x0​, which says that the left limit equals the value of the function at the threshold:

lim⁡e→0+E[Y0∣X=x0−e]=E[Y0∣X=x0]\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y_0|X=x_0-e]=E[Y_0|X=x_0]e→0+lim​E[Y0​∣X=x0​−e]=E[Y0​∣X=x0​]

Therefore

E[Y∣X=x0]−lim⁡e→0+E[Y∣X=x0−e]=E[Y1∣X=x0]−E[Y0∣X=x0]=E[Y1−Y0∣X=x0]\begin{aligned} E[Y|X=x_0]-\lim_{e\to0^+}E[Y|X=x_0-e]&=E[Y_1|X=x_0]-E[Y_0|X=x_0]\\ &=E[Y_1-Y_0|X=x_0] \end{aligned}E[Y∣X=x0​]−e→0+lim​E[Y∣X=x0​−e]​=E[Y1​∣X=x0​]−E[Y0​∣X=x0​]=E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=x0​]​

Only the continuity of E[Y0∣X=x]E[Y_0|X=x]E[Y0​∣X=x] is used here, because treated units are observed at x0x_0x0​ itself; continuity of E[Y1∣X=x]E[Y_1|X=x]E[Y1​∣X=x] would be needed if the threshold point were untreated. The argument needs observations with XXX arbitrarily close to x0x_0x0​ from below. With JJJ support points the nearest untreated cell is xk−1x_{k-1}xk−1​, and the analogue E[Y∣X=0]−E[Y∣X=xk−1]E[Y|X=0]-E[Y|X=x_{k-1}]E[Y∣X=0]−E[Y∣X=xk−1​] equals the treatment effect plus E[Y0∣X=0]−E[Y0∣X=xk−1]E[Y_0|X=0]-E[Y_0|X=x_{k-1}]E[Y0​∣X=0]−E[Y0​∣X=xk−1​], a term that no amount of data removes.

This is the identifying assumption for a discrete covariate. The index j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J runs over the support points of XXX, with the threshold cell normalized to xk=0x_k=0xk​=0, and Dj=1[xj≥0]D_j=1[x_j\geq0]Dj​=1[xj​≥0] is the treatment status of cell jjj. The function h(⋅)h(\cdot)h(⋅) is the continuous part of the regression function, and β0\beta_0β0​ is the size of the jump at zero.

The normalization h(0)=E[Y0∣X=0]h(0)=E[Y_0|X=0]h(0)=E[Y0​∣X=0] gives the jump its causal meaning. Evaluating the equation at the threshold cell, where Dk=1D_k=1Dk​=1 and the observed outcome is Y1Y_1Y1​:

E[Y1∣X=0]=E[Y∣X=0]=β0+h(0)=β0+E[Y0∣X=0]⟹β0=E[Y1−Y0∣X=0]E[Y_1|X=0]=E[Y|X=0]=\beta_0+h(0)=\beta_0+E[Y_0|X=0]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta_0=E[Y_1-Y_0|X=0]E[Y1​∣X=0]=E[Y∣X=0]=β0​+h(0)=β0​+E[Y0​∣X=0]⟹β0​=E[Y1​−Y0​∣X=0]

As written, with hhh unrestricted, the equation has no content: any JJJ numbers E[Y∣X=xj]E[Y|X=x_j]E[Y∣X=xj​] can be fitted by a continuous hhh and an arbitrary β0\beta_0β0​, because a continuous function can connect E[Y∣X=xk−1]E[Y|X=x_{k-1}]E[Y∣X=xk−1​] to any value of h(0)h(0)h(0). The equation identifies β0\beta_0β0​ only when hhh is restricted to a family with fewer than JJJ free parameters, in practice a low-order polynomial. Then β0\beta_0β0​ is obtained by extrapolating hhh from the untreated cells x1,…,xk−1x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}x1​,…,xk−1​ to 000. Everything that follows is about the consequences of that extrapolation being imperfect: equation (7) introduces the deviation aja_jaj​ of hhh from the polynomial, and equations (13) to (16) ask whether the deviation is the same for the two potential outcomes.

This is equation (3) written for individual observations. YijY_{ij}Yij​ is the outcome of individual i=1,…,nji=1,\ldots,n_ji=1,…,nj​ in cell jjj, and the error is defined as the deviation from the cell expectation, εij≡Yij−E[Yij∣X=xj]\varepsilon_{ij}\equiv Y_{ij}-E[Y_{ij}|X=x_j]εij​≡Yij​−E[Yij​∣X=xj​]. By construction E[εij∣X=xj]=0E[\varepsilon_{ij}|X=x_j]=0E[εij​∣X=xj​]=0, so the equation is not an additional assumption; it only names the within-cell sampling variation. Its conditional variance σεj2\sigma^2_{\varepsilon j}σεj2​ may differ across cells.

The distinction that matters later is between two sources of noise. Averaging the equation within a cell gives

Y‾j=Djβ0+h(xj)+ε‾j,V(ε‾j)=σεj2nj\overline{Y}_j=D_j\beta_0+h(x_j)+\overline{\varepsilon}_j,\qquad V(\overline{\varepsilon}_j)=\frac{\sigma^2_{\varepsilon j}}{n_j}Yj​=Dj​β0​+h(xj​)+εj​,V(εj​)=nj​σεj2​​

so the sampling error εij\varepsilon_{ij}εij​ averages out as the cell grows, and with large cells the JJJ points E[Y∣X=xj]E[Y|X=x_j]E[Y∣X=xj​] are known almost exactly. What does not average out is any error in the functional form of hhh, which is common to all individuals of the cell; that component is introduced in equation (7). The unrestricted version of this equation, with a separate mean for each cell, is the regression on JJJ dummies that produces ESSURESS_{UR}ESSUR​ in equation (5); a polynomial for hhh produces ESSRESS_RESSR​.

GGG is the classical FFF statistic for testing the polynomial model (the restricted model, with KKK parameters including the intercept and the coefficient on DjD_jDj​) against the saturated model with one mean per support point (JJJ parameters). The test has J−KJ-KJ−K restrictions, and ESSUR/(N−J)ESS_{UR}/(N-J)ESSUR​/(N−J) is the usual unbiased estimator of the sampling variance. This is the form printed as equation (3) of the paper.

Because the regressors are constant within cells, the sums of squares have a transparent cell-mean form. The unrestricted fitted value is Y‾j\overline{Y}_jYj​, and for each cell ∑i(Yij−Wjθ^)2=∑i(Yij−Y‾j)2+nj(Y‾j−Wjθ^)2\sum_i(Y_{ij}-W_j\hat{\theta})^2=\sum_i(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j)^2+n_j(\overline{Y}_j-W_j\hat{\theta})^2∑i​(Yij​−Wj​θ^)2=∑i​(Yij​−Yj​)2+nj​(Yj​−Wj​θ^)2, since the cross term sums to zero. Hence

ESSUR=∑j=1J∑i=1nj(Yij−Y‾j)2,ESSR−ESSUR=∑j=1Jnj(Y‾j−Wjθ^)2ESS_{UR}=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\left(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j\right)^2,\qquad ESS_R-ESS_{UR}=\sum_{j=1}^Jn_j\left(\overline{Y}_j-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2ESSUR​=j=1∑J​i=1∑nj​​(Yij​−Yj​)2,ESSR​−ESSUR​=j=1∑J​nj​(Yj​−Wj​θ^)2

The numerator of GGG measures how far the cell means are from the fitted polynomial, the denominator how noisy the cell means are expected to be. If the polynomial is exactly right (aj=0a_j=0aj​=0 in equation (7)) and εij\varepsilon_{ij}εij​ is normal and homoskedastic, the two quadratic forms are independent chi-squares divided by their degrees of freedom and G∼F(J−K,N−J)G\sim F(J-K,N-J)G∼F(J−K,N−J) exactly; without normality (J−K)G(J-K)G(J−K)G is asymptotically χ2(J−K)\chi^2(J-K)χ2(J−K) as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞ with JJJ fixed. Under the null E[G]E[G]E[G] is close to 1, and values well above 1 signal specification error. These distributional statements hold under the null of no specification error. The cell-mean identity is used again in equations (12) and (20), where G−1G-1G−1 turns out to be proportional to an estimate of the variance of the specification error.

A remark on notation: here KKK counts all parameters of the restricted model, whereas in the appendix sequence of equation (21) the same letter denotes the number of polynomial columns of XXX only.

The paper defines the heteroskedasticity-robust statistic as a weighted version of ESSR−ESSURESS_R-ESS_{UR}ESSR​−ESSUR​, with each observation of cell jjj weighted by 1/σ^εj21/\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}1/σ^εj2​:

G~≡∑j=1J∑i=1nj1σ^εj2(Yij−Wjθ^)2−∑j=1J∑i=1nj1σ^εj2(Yij−Y‾j)2\tilde{G}\equiv\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\frac{1}{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}}\left(Y_{ij}-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2-\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\frac{1}{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}}\left(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j\right)^2G~≡j=1∑J​i=1∑nj​​σ^εj2​1​(Yij​−Wj​θ^)2−j=1∑J​i=1∑nj​​σ^εj2​1​(Yij​−Yj​)2

Step 1 decomposes the first inner sum around the cell mean. The cross term vanishes because ∑i(Yij−Y‾j)=0\sum_i(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j)=0∑i​(Yij​−Yj​)=0:

∑i=1nj(Yij−Wjθ^)2=∑i=1nj(Yij−Y‾j)2+nj(Y‾j−Wjθ^)2\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\left(Y_{ij}-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\left(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j\right)^2+n_j\left(\overline{Y}_j-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2i=1∑nj​​(Yij​−Wj​θ^)2=i=1∑nj​​(Yij​−Yj​)2+nj​(Yj​−Wj​θ^)2

Step 2 substitutes. The within-cell sums of squares cancel and the cell-mean form of the note remains:

G~=∑j=1Jnjσ^εj2(Y‾j−Wjθ^)2\tilde{G}=\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{n_j}{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}}\left(\overline{Y}_j-W_j\hat{\theta}\right)^2G~=j=1∑J​σ^εj2​nj​​(Yj​−Wj​θ^)2

Step 3 notes that, with σ^εj2=(1/nj)∑i(Yij−Y‾j)2\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}=(1/n_j)\sum_i(Y_{ij}-\overline{Y}_j)^2σ^εj2​=(1/nj​)∑i​(Yij​−Yj​)2, the subtracted term equals ∑jnj=N\sum_jn_j=N∑j​nj​=N, which gives the third equivalent form in the paper, the weighted restricted sum of squares minus NNN. The divisor njn_jnj​ (not nj−1n_j-1nj​−1) is what makes this exact.

Step 4 gives the distribution. As nj→∞n_j\to\inftynj​→∞ with JJJ fixed and no specification error, zj≡nj(Y‾j−E[Y∣X=xj])/σεjz_j\equiv\sqrt{n_j}(\overline{Y}_j-E[Y|X=x_j])/\sigma_{\varepsilon j}zj​≡nj​​(Yj​−E[Y∣X=xj​])/σεj​ are independent and asymptotically N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1), and

G~=∑j=1J(zj−njσεjWj(θ^−θ0))2+op(1)\tilde{G}=\sum_{j=1}^J\left(z_j-\frac{\sqrt{n_j}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon j}}W_j(\hat{\theta}-\theta_0)\right)^2+o_p(1)G~=j=1∑J​(zj​−σεj​nj​​​Wj​(θ^−θ0​))2+op​(1)

This is a minimum-distance (minimum chi-square) criterion. It is the squared length of the residual from projecting the JJJ-vector zzz on the KKK columns of the rescaled regressor matrix, and therefore χ2(J−K)\chi^2(J-K)χ2(J−K), when θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ minimizes the same weighted criterion, that is, when θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ is the least squares estimator weighted by 1/σ^εj21/\hat{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon j}1/σ^εj2​ per observation. This is the device that makes the asymptotic approximation behave sensibly. It is an assumption on a hypothetical sequence of designs indexed by JJJ, not a description of data. X∗X^*X∗ is a J×KJ\times KJ×K random matrix of polynomial terms with fixed distribution, and DDD is the J×2J\times2J×2 matrix whose rows DjD_jDj​ contain the constant and the treatment indicator. instead of growing like JJJ. What this buys: γ^−γ\hat{\gamma}-\gammaγ^​−γ is Op(1)O_p(1)Op​(1), and so the estimated discontinuity, which depends on γ^\hat{\gamma}γ^​ through the extrapolation to the threshold, has an estimation error of order 1, the same order as the forecast error a1k−a0ka_{1k}-a_{0k}a1k​−a0k​ of equation (16). Both components then survive in the limit and equation (17) holds for every σa2≥0\sigma^2_a\geq0σa2​≥0, with a variance that is continuous at σa2=0\sigma^2_a=0σa2​=0. Under conventional asymptotics the estimation error would be Op(1/J)O_p(1/\sqrt{J})Op​(1/J​) and would vanish next to the forecast error. The device is the analogue of local-to-zero sequences used elsewhere in econometrics (weak instruments, local alternatives): parameters are drifted with the sample size so that the limit keeps a feature of the finite sample. Equations (22) and (23) work out the consequences. Note that in this block KKK is the number of columns of XXX, while in equation (5) it is the total number of restricted parameters.

This is the fuzzy design, written as a two-equation system for cell jjj and individual iii. In this block the subscripts 1 and 2 label equations, not potential outcomes: Y1ijY_{1ij}Y1ij​ is the treatment actually received (class size, programme participation) and Y2ijY_{2ij}Y2ij​ the outcome. The first line is a first stage: the expected treatment jumps by δ0\delta_0δ0​ at the threshold but is otherwise a smooth polynomial Xjγ1X_j\gamma_1Xj​γ1​. The second line is the structural equation: β0\beta_0β0​ is the causal effect of Y1Y_1Y1​ on Y2Y_2Y2​, and the exclusion restriction is that DjD_jDj​ does not appear in it. The individual errors (uij,vij)(u_{ij},v_{ij})(uij​,vij​) may be correlated, which is why least squares on the second line is inconsistent; (a1j,a2j)(a_{1j},a_{2j})(a1j​,a2j​) are cell-level specification errors of the two polynomials, mean zero and i.i.d. across cells.

Substituting the first line into the second gives the reduced form for the outcome,

so the discontinuity in the outcome is δ0β0\delta_0\beta_0δ0​β0​, and the instrumental variables estimator with instrument DjD_jDj​ is the ratio of the two discontinuities,

Both the first stage and the reduced form have the random-effects structure of equation (7), with cell-level errors a1ja_{1j}a1j​ and a1jβ0+a2ja_{1j}\beta_0+a_{2j}a1j​β0​+a2j​. Hence the conventional instrumental variables standard errors understate the variance for the same reason as in equations (10) and (11), and clustering on the values of XXX is the remedy. The system treats the specification errors as the same on both sides of the threshold (the identical-errors case of equation (14)); the independent-errors case leads to equation (31).

Apply the sharp-design analysis separately to the two outcomes Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y2Y_2Y2​. By the argument for equation (17), applied jointly, the estimation errors are asymptotically bivariate normal, the forecast errors are bivariate normal by assumption, and the two vectors are asymptotically independent. Replacing Σ\SigmaΣ by a consistent estimator Σ^\hat{\Sigma}Σ^ does not change the limit (Slutsky), which gives the displayed result. The set of pairs of discontinuities for which the quadratic form is below 5.99, the 0.95 quantile of χ2(2)\chi^2(2)χ2(2), is a joint confidence ellipse; the set of ratios of second to first coordinate over the ellipse is a confidence set for the fuzzy-design effect, conservative because it is a projection, and unbounded if the ellipse touches a zero first-stage discontinuity. The paper states this result as a sketch, without a formal proof.
